question: Is it better to refinish or replace hardwood floors?
title: Refinish or Replace Hardwood Floors: Which Pays Off?
h1: Should You Refinish Your Hardwood Floors or Replace Them?
description: Refinishing runs $2-$8/sq ft versus $9-$25/sq ft for new hardwood, and recovered 147% of cost at resale versus 118% for new wood per NAR/NARI 2022.
capsule: For Sarasota and Manatee County homeowners, refinishing existing hardwood typically costs $2-$8 per sq ft, versus $9-$25 per sq ft installed for new hardwood - refinishing wins on cost when the floor is structurally sound. The NAR/NARI 2022 Remodeling Impact Report found hardwood refinishing recovered 147% of its cost at resale, versus 118% for new wood flooring.

The math usually favors refinishing when it's an option, since it's typically a fraction of what new hardwood costs installed. That gap holds for both a solid and an engineered replacement comparison - refinishing an existing floor almost never costs more than putting in new engineered hardwood over the same square footage. See our full hardwood cost guide for how those installed numbers break down by plank width and species.

Cost alone doesn't decide this question, though it's usually the first thing homeowners ask about. A floor has to have enough wood left in the wear layer to sand - a solid 3/4 in. board can usually take about 4 full sandings over its life, while engineered floors are limited by wear layer thickness, often only 1-4 sandings depending on the product. See our guide on how many times a floor can be refinished for the specifics. Water damage that's warped or rotted boards, or cupping that hasn't been corrected at the moisture source, both need repair or replacement rather than a straight sand-and-refinish. If a floor has already been sanded close to its limit, another full sand risks sanding through to the tongue-and-groove or the plywood core underneath. Subfloor problems change the equation too - if the boards themselves are fine but the floor underneath has settled or shifted, that's a repair or leveling issue to solve before either refinishing or replacing makes sense, and it's worth fixing regardless of which flooring path you choose afterward.

sections.h2: Which one pays back more at resale
sections.html: The NAR/NARI 2022 Remodeling Impact Report - a joint survey of real estate agents and homeowners on which projects recoup their cost at sale - found that refinishing hardwood floors recovered about 147% of its cost, while installing new wood flooring recovered about 118%. Both come back above 100%, meaning buyers generally value hardwood floors more than either project costs at the time of resale, but refinishing came out ahead in that particular survey. Note that the 2025 edition of the same report didn't include a flooring category at all, so this remains the most recent flooring-specific data publicly available. That's worth keeping in mind for anyone weighing this decision against replacing floors before selling a house in Sarasota or Manatee County - especially since refinishing is also the faster project to complete before a listing goes live.

sections.h2: How to decide for your floor
sections.html: We start every refinish-or-replace call with a walkthrough: checking remaining wear layer or board thickness, looking for water damage or structural issues, and confirming the subfloor underneath is sound. If the floor passes that check, refinishing is almost always the lower-cost, faster path to the look of a new floor. If it doesn't, we'll say so - a quote for new hardwood over a subfloor that needs work first is more honest than pushing a refinish that won't hold up. Book a free estimate and we'll check the floor in person before recommending either path. Bring any history you have on the floor - when it was installed, whether it's been sanded before, and any known water events - since that context speeds up the assessment and helps us give you an honest answer on the first visit rather than a second trip.

faqs.q: Does refinishing look as good as new hardwood?
faqs.a: A well-executed sand-and-refinish on a sound floor can look essentially like new, since it removes the old finish and any surface scratches down to bare, even-colored wood before the new coats go on.

faqs.q: Can I refinish just part of my floor instead of the whole house?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if the area is isolated and the color and sheen can be matched to the surrounding floor. Refinishing typically looks most consistent when done as one continuous area rather than patched room by room.

faqs.q: What's the newest data on flooring's resale return?
faqs.a: The NAR/NARI Remodeling Impact Report last covered flooring projects in its 2022 edition; the 2025 edition doesn't include a flooring category, so 2022 remains the most recent sourced figure.
